name: Weighing-Stone Primer (Quyền Thạch Quyết)
concept: The outer gate's method, practised with a stone weight in each open palm. Metal qi is drawn into the right pan and Earth into the left until the beam of the body lies level; a root that holds only one element fills one pan and must carry the other by effort, which is slow but not closed. Each layer adds a heavier pair of weights from the rack on Thạch Quyền Phong. The sixth layer is the Level Beam: the disciple stands on the great scale of the outer gate holding the master's weights, and if the beam does not tip for the time it takes an incense stick to burn, and their Metal is strong enough to take the Dipper Handle, the inner gate opens.
lore: Chung Hoài Cực wrote it in 230 for the ore miners of Ngọc Hành Sơn, the first outsiders to come in under the Pivot's protection (C059). They knew weights better than letters, so he wrote a method that could be taught on a market scale. The outer gate's scale on Thạch Quyền Phong is the oldest in the sect, older than the one at Thiên Quyền Thị (A207).

name: Dipper Handle Canon (Đẩu Bính Kinh)
concept: The inner gate's method. The Dipper's handle turns once a year around a still pole and points the season: east for spring, south for summer. The cultivator turns Metal qi around a fixed centre below the navel, one star at a time. In a fight each Metal art cast moves the handle one star; at the seventh star the handle points, and the next Metal art lands twice. A disciple who rushes it, firing an art that is not Metal or two arts within a breath of each other, loses count: the stars fall away, and the handle turns again only after he has stayed Composed for three seconds. That is the first lesson the inner gate teaches: the order of things is the power.
lore: Written by Chung Hoài Cực in the 260s, after the watchmen on Trích Tinh Phong reported that one could pluck the stars by hand (A084). The founder said the line he took from it was that the stars are near but do not come when called. The first copy is cut into the stone of Xu Trụ Phong, seven columns for the seven stars.

name: Heavenly Pivot True Canon (Thiên Xu Chân Kinh)

effects.name: The Pole Draws from the Vein (Xu Cực Dẫn Mạch)
effects.rule: A passive art (authored wish d8). While you are Composed, you regain 0.2 % of your maximum linh lực each second for every 3 Earth stacks (Weights) on the foe, rounded down. Its engine record is the Effect of the same name in effects/thien_xu.effects.json; the loader does not yet attach a technique's Effects (pending word technique-effects).

concept: The founder's method and the sect's name. Thiên Xu is the first star of the Dipper, the one the others turn on. The holder becomes the fixed point. While they stay Composed, their flying edges and their arrays orbit them, and the foe is weighed: each hit lays a Weight (an Earth stack), and Metal arts strike harder on a foe who carries more Weight. The method rewards patience and punishes the holder for Pressing: it costs the Weights already laid. Every head has fought from one spot.
lore: Chung Hoài Cực wrote it at 80, the year he founded the sect under the Northern Dipper (C002), and rewrote its last three layers after the War of the Pivot (C106). The rewritten layers teach the holder to stop a war without winning it. Only two people have cultivated past the twelfth layer, the founder and Đỗ Tinh Hà. Doãn Ngọc Hành has been at the tenth for forty years.

name: Boundary Stele Array Canon (Giới Bi Trận Kinh)
concept: The arrays of the Compact's boundary steles. A stele planted in the ground is an anchor, and an array strung between two anchors becomes a line no one crosses without being felt. The 129 steles the Pivot keeps along the borders of the seven great sects are one great array of this kind, and the Thiên Cơ Hall walks them every ten years. In a fight the holder gains Stele charges, each dearer than the last while others are held; while two are held, the foe is slowed and takes Earth stacks, and the holder holds a ward.
lore: The first master of the Thiên Cơ Hall wrote it in 511-515 to plant the steles of the North Star Compact (C107). When the avalanche buried Thủ Bi Trại in 1006 the stele it guarded was moved lower (V129), and the array has carried a small kink there ever since. The hall knows; it has not been mended.

name: Army-Breaker Spear (Phá Quân Thương Quyết)
concept: Phá Quân Môn's spear art, named for the Dipper's seventh star. The spearman waits. Each second without striking builds Momentum, which loses a twentieth of itself each second, each second of waiting past the fifth costs 1 % of the holder's linh lực, and the next thrust spends all of it at once. The art teaches a long stillness and one called, killing blow, which is why it suits a war marshal and not a duelist. Its last layers teach the spear to strike a formation at its weakest file, and teach the marshal to let the army fight: hits by his companions, his flying blades and his formation are not his, so they keep his wait and add Momentum to it.
lore: Taken with Hạ Lang Tinh's spear when Thiên Xu destroyed Phá Quân Môn in 874 (C163). Đỗ Tinh Hà made it the art of the Dao Quang Hall, saying that an art is not guilty of its owner's rebellion. The elders of the Thiên Quyền Hall have argued against that for three centuries.

name: Water-Clock Breathing (Lậu Khắc Thổ Nạp Pháp)
concept: The seat's servants' method for the roots the Primer cannot weigh. There is no music at the seat and no bell but the one at dusk, so time is kept by the water clock, and the servants who tend it learned to breathe with its drip: one breath in for a drop, one out for the next, Water drawn in with the cold mountain air and Wood with the scented smoke of the hall's fires. It keeps a body steady and a breath unhurried through the long plateau winters, and it opens no gate.
lore: No elder wrote it. The keepers of the water clock passed it down by mouth since the clock was set up after the War of the Nine Shao (C005), and Hà Khắc Thủy teaches it now to any servant whose root the Level Beam cannot read.
